extraction.name: Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD)
extraction.description: SQuAD is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text (span) from the corresponding reading passage. SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar, Jian Zhang, Konstantin Lopyrev, Percy Liang (Stanford University)
extraction.citeAs: Rajpurkar, P., Zhang, J., Lopyrev, K., & Liang, P. (2016). SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text. arXiv:1606.05250v3 [cs.CL].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected in three stages: (1) Passage curation: top 10,000 Wikipedia articles by PageRank were obtained, 536 articles were sampled uniformly at random, and paragraphs shorter than 500 characters or containing images/figures/tables were discarded, resulting in 23,215 paragraphs. (2) Question-answer collection: crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions per paragraph, with answers highlighted as spans in the paragraph text. (3) Additional answers collection: at least 2 additional answers were obtained for each question in the development and test sets to assess human performance and robustness.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers during the secondary answer generation task.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Top 10,000 English Wikipedia articles ranked by Project Nayuki's Wikipedia internal PageRanks. 536 articles were sampled uniformly at random, and individual paragraphs were extracted from these articles.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Articles were partitioned randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%). Images, figures, tables were stripped from articles, and paragraphs shorter than 500 characters were discarded.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Paragraphs were extracted from Wikipedia articles by stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. Constituency parses and POS tags were generated using Stanford CoreNLP for answer categorization. NER tags were used to further classify proper noun phrases into person, location, and other entities. Candidate answers were restricted to constituents in the constituency parse; during training, when the correct answer was not a constituent, the shortest constituent containing the correct answer was used as the target.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were asked to spend 4 minutes on every paragraph and asked to ask and answer up to 5 questions on the content of each paragraph. Questions had to be entered in a text field, and answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph. Workers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words without copying word phrases from the paragraph; copy-paste functionality on the paragraph text was disabled. For additional answers, each crowdworker was shown only the questions along with the paragraphs and asked to select the shortest span in the paragraph that answered the question. If a question was not answerable by a span, workers submitted the question without marking an answer.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform (with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend)
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was assessed by treating the second answer to each question as the human prediction and keeping the other answers as ground truth. The resulting human performance on the test set is 77.0% exact match and 86.8% F1. Mismatch occurs mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases rather than fundamental disagreements. 192 examples were manually labeled into reasoning categories to understand the types of reasoning required.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in the development and test sets (1 original + at least 2 additional); training set questions have 1 answer each.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford CoreNLP (for constituency parses, POS tags, NER tags, and dependency parse trees)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is versioned (v1.0 and v1.1 mentioned in the paper). The dataset is freely available at https://stanford-qa.com. No explicit deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive progress in machine reading comprehension and natural language understanding. By providing a large, high-quality benchmark, it aims to enable development of more expressive statistical and neural models for reading comprehension.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Crowdworkers were required to be located in the United States or Canada, which may introduce geographic and linguistic bias. The dataset is based on top Wikipedia articles by PageRank, which may over-represent certain topics. Questions were posed by crowdworkers who may have particular question-asking styles.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Answers are constrained to be spans of text from the passage, which is more constrained than free-form answers. 77.3% of correct answers are constituents in the constituency parse, placing an effective ceiling on methods relying on constituency parsing. The dataset does not provide answer choices, requiring systems to select from all possible spans. Some questions (2.6% in dev/test) were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development (validation), and testing of machine reading comprehension models. The dataset is intended for use in training and evaluating models that answer questions by selecting spans from a given passage. It is freely available to encourage exploration of expressive models for reading comprehension.
